title: Vaping Harms the Heart Too, Not Just the Lungs, Doctors Warn
excerpt: Growing research shows e-cigarettes expose users to chemicals that damage blood vessels and disrupt heart rhythm — and a new expert consensus says no nicotine product is safe for the heart.
body:
• A growing body of research shows e-cigarettes expose users to chemicals that can harm the heart and blood vessels, according to the American Heart Association.
  • Nicotine is a direct cardiovascular toxin — raising blood pressure and heart rate, narrowing blood vessels, promoting clots and damaging vessel function — regardless of whether it comes from cigarettes, vapes or pouches.
  • A June 2026 study found synthetic cooling chemicals in some e-cigarettes can disrupt heart rhythm, raising the risk of irregular heartbeat and cardiac arrest.
  • An expert consensus report in the European Heart Journal concluded there is "no such thing as 'safer nicotine'" for the heart.

Vaping is often treated as a harmless alternative to smoking — a safer habit for people trying to quit. Doctors and researchers say the heart tells a different story: a growing body of evidence shows e-cigarettes expose users to chemicals that can harm the heart and blood vessels, not just the lungs.

The American Heart Association warned in June 2026 that e-cigarette aerosol, often misrepresented as harmless water vapor, contains a mix of chemicals, additives, sweeteners and flavoring agents that the US Food and Drug Administration classifies as harmful or potentially harmful. "A growing body of research shows that people who use e-cigarettes can be exposed to chemicals that can harm the heart and blood vessels," said Dr. Jason J. Rose, an AHA volunteer and associate professor at the University of Maryland School of Medicine, who chaired the AHA's 2023 scientific statement on e-cigarettes.

Context & Background

The concern is not just nicotine, though nicotine itself is central. A major expert consensus report published in the European Heart Journal concluded that nicotine is a direct cardiovascular toxin across every delivery method — cigarettes, vapes, heated tobacco and nicotine pouches. "Nicotine is not a harmless stimulant; it is a direct cardiovascular toxin," said lead researcher Dr. Thomas Münzel, senior professor of cardiology at Johannes Gutenberg University in Mainz, Germany. "No product that delivers nicotine is safe for the heart."

Beyond nicotine, vaping introduces its own chemical risks. Research shows e-cigarettes expose users to formaldehyde and heavy metals linked to cardiovascular harm. In a study published in June 2026 in Circulation: Arrhythmia and Electrophysiology, researchers found that synthetic cooling chemicals used in some e-cigarettes may disrupt heart rhythm, pointing to potential risks such as irregular heartbeat and cardiac arrest.

"Nicotine is not a harmless stimulant; it is a direct cardiovascular toxin. Across cigarettes, vapes, heated tobacco and nicotine pouches, we consistently see increased blood pressure, damage to blood vessels and a higher risk of heart disease."

— Dr. Thomas Münzel, University Medical Center Mainz

Impact & Analysis

The cardiovascular research on vaping is still catching up with the product's popularity, but the early signals point to real vascular damage. Studies comparing chronic e-cigarette users, smokers and non-users found that both vapers and smokers had impaired flow-mediated dilation — how well blood vessels relax in response to increased blood flow — an established early warning sign of cardiovascular disease. Vaping also caused a specific effect that smoking did not: it increased the permeability of small blood vessels, suggesting a vaping-specific mechanism of vascular harm.

A meta-analysis found that exclusive e-cigarette use had a similar impact on one key marker of arterial stiffness as exclusive cigarette smoking — a sobering finding, since arterial stiffening is linked to heart attack and stroke risk. Dual users — people who both vape and smoke — fared worst, with roughly doubled odds of cardiovascular disease compared to never-users.

Researchers still consider e-cigarettes likely less harmful than combustible cigarettes for a smoker switching completely — but "less harmful than smoking" is not harmless, and for never-smokers who take up vaping, the risks come with none of the comparative benefits.

Diaspora Angle

The warning lands with particular relevance for Indian families. Vaping is banned in India under the 2019 prohibition on e-cigarettes, yet the devices remain widely available, especially to young people — and diaspora households in the US and UK navigate a different regulatory landscape where flavored vapes have targeted youth aggressively. Doctors advise parents to treat vaping as a genuine cardiovascular risk, not a phase, and to watch for it in teenagers whose routine checkups are not designed to catch early vessel damage.

What's Next

Long-term studies are still needed to quantify vaping's full cardiovascular toll — e-cigarettes are too new for the decades-long tracking that settled the science on smoking. In the meantime, the practical guidance from cardiologists is straightforward: if you smoke, switching to vaping may reduce harm but quitting nicotine entirely is the goal; if you don't smoke, don't start vaping. Anyone with concerns about their heart should speak to a doctor rather than assuming a vape habit is benign.
